content: When planning international travel, individuals often consult healthcare professionals for advice on necessary vaccinations. This consultation provides an opportunity to review the traveler’s vaccination history and administer any required primary series or booster doses. In many countries, diseases such as measles, mumps, and rubella remain uncontrolled. Consequently, the risk of contracting these diseases while traveling outside the United States is significantly higher than within the country. Between 1985 and 1989, approximately 61% of imported measles cases in the U.S. occurred among returning citizens. To reduce the risk of importing diseases, all international travelers should be immune to measles. Individuals born in or after 1957 who are traveling abroad and lack evidence of immunity or have not received two doses of the measles vaccine should receive a dose of the vaccine. Evidence of immunity includes a history of physician-diagnosed measles or laboratory confirmation of immunity. If travelers are also susceptible to mumps or rubella, the MMR vaccine is recommended. In developed countries such as Japan, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, and European nations, the risk of contracting vaccine-preventable diseases like polio, diphtheria, and tetanus is generally no greater than the risk within the United States. Unvaccinated adults traveling to developing countries or regions with endemic polio should receive at least two doses of inactivated poliovirus vaccine (IPV) one month apart, ideally completing the primary series before travel. IPV is preferred due to the slightly higher risk of vaccine-associated paralysis in adults compared to children. If time constraints prevent completion of the series, a single dose of either oral poliovirus vaccine (OPV) or IPV is recommended. Adults who have not completed their primary polio vaccination series should receive the remaining doses, regardless of the interval since the last dose or the type of vaccine previously administered. Travelers who have completed a primary series of OPV should receive a single supplementary dose of OPV, while those who completed an IPV series should receive a supplementary dose of either OPV or IPV. The necessity for additional doses has not been established. Individuals at increased risk of complications from influenza, such as those with certain health conditions, should review their influenza vaccination history before traveling to the tropics at any time of year or to the Southern Hemisphere between April and September. If they were not vaccinated during the previous fall or winter, they should consider receiving the influenza vaccine before travel. High-risk individuals should be encouraged to receive the most current vaccine available. Those vaccinated with the previous season’s vaccine in preparation for travel should be revaccinated in the fall or winter with the current vaccine, potentially receiving two doses within one year. Selective vaccination against diseases such as yellow fever, cholera, typhoid, plague, meningococcal disease, rabies, or hepatitis B, or the administration of immune globulin (IG) for hepatitis A prevention, is recommended based on the specific disease risks in the destination country and the type and duration of travel. For yellow fever and cholera, vaccination requirements may be mandated by the destination country. Information on countries reporting yellow fever, cholera, and plague is updated biweekly in the Summary of Health Information for International Travel. Additional details on vaccine-preventable illnesses are provided in sections describing specific vaccines. Foreign students, immigrants, and refugees entering the United States may be susceptible to diseases such as diphtheria, tetanus, measles, mumps, rubella, and polio, as routine vaccination against these diseases is not universal in many countries. Refugees from regions with high hepatitis B virus (HBV) endemicity, such as Southeast Asia, should be screened for hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) and anti-HBs. Susceptible household and sexual contacts of HBsAg carriers should receive the HBV vaccine. Unless foreign students, immigrants, and refugees can provide documented evidence of vaccination or immunity, they should receive age-appropriate vaccines as outlined in the Age Groups section and corresponding tables. Certain vaccines may be contraindicated for individuals with specific health conditions, while others may be indicated due to underlying health issues. Pregnant women should delay vaccination until the second or third trimester when possible to minimize concerns about potential teratogenicity. Pregnant women not previously vaccinated against tetanus and diphtheria should receive two properly spaced doses of Td vaccine. Those who have received one or two doses should complete the primary series during pregnancy. A primary series consists of three doses of diphtheria and tetanus toxoids, with the first two doses given at least four weeks apart and the third dose administered 6–12 months after the second. Pregnant women who have completed a primary series should receive a Td booster if more than 10 years have elapsed since their last dose. Live-virus vaccines are generally contraindicated during pregnancy due to a theoretical risk to the developing fetus.
